architectures.name: Priority queues per channel with dedicated workers
architectures.summary: An ingestion API writes validated requests to durable queues separated by channel and priority. Channel workers apply preferences and templates, call providers through rate limiters, and record status.
architectures.bestWhen: Different channels have different providers, limits, and failure modes, and critical traffic must be isolated from bulk traffic.
drawbacks: More queues and consumer groups to operate.
Cross-channel coordination, such as push then SMS fallback, needs an explicit orchestrator.

architectures.name: Workflow orchestration for multi-step notifications
architectures.summary: A workflow or state-machine engine drives each notification through preference check, rendering, send, wait for receipt, and fallback channel steps.
architectures.bestWhen: Notifications involve conditional logic such as escalation or fallback across channels and per-notification state is valuable.
drawbacks: Higher per-message overhead compared with plain queues.
Engine becomes a critical dependency and scaling limit.
Harder to reason about at very high volume without batching.

architectures.name: Fan-out service for bulk campaigns
architectures.summary: Campaign requests are expanded by a fan-out service that reads audience segments in pages and enqueues individual messages at a controlled rate, while transactional traffic uses a separate low-latency path.
architectures.bestWhen: Large campaigns dominate volume and must not interfere with transactional messages.
drawbacks: Campaign cancellation and progress tracking add complexity.
Audience changes during a long-running send need a defined policy.
